The big idea

When you get the challenge, do not start coding immediately.

First, look at the picture and ask:

What does one bar/point/line represent?

That one question tells you what your final cleaned data needs to look like.

For example, in your dealership challenge, each bar represented:

one dealership’s total sales in one year

So your final data needed one row per:

year + dealership

and a number column:

total_sold

That is why the final data needed to look like:

year	dealership	total_sold
2017	BEACON	270
2017	DRAPER	406
2018	BEACON	253
2018	DRAPER	373

The graph becomes much easier once you know what one row of the final plotting data should represent.

Your general test process

Use this order almost every time:

library(tidyverse)

data <- read_csv("...")

glimpse(data)
View(data)
names(data)

Then ask:

Are the column names clean?
Is the data wide or long?
Do I need to create a date/year/month column?
Do I need to filter rows?
Do I need to group and summarize?
What goes into ggplot(aes())?
What geom_ matches the picture?

That is your whole battle plan.

Scenario 1: Wide data that needs pivot_longer()

This is what happened with your dealership challenge.

You see data like:

quarter	BEACON	DRAPER	FILMORE
2017 Q1	69	130	85
2017 Q2	77	86	97

The dealership names are currently column names.

But in a nice tidy dataset, dealership should be its own column.

So you use:

data_long <- data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -quarter,
    names_to = "dealership",
    values_to = "cars_sold"
  )

Read that in English:

cols = -quarter

means:

Take every column except quarter.

names_to = "dealership"

means:

Put the old column names into a new column called dealership.

values_to = "cars_sold"

means:

Put the numbers into a new column called cars_sold.

You use pivot_longer() when the column names are secretly values.

Examples:

Bad/wide columns	What they really are
BEACON, DRAPER, FILMORE	dealership names
Male, Female	gender values
2019, 2020, 2021	year values
January, February, March	month values
Math, Science, English	subject values

Pattern:

data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = columns_to_stack,
    names_to = "new_category_column",
    values_to = "new_number_column"
  )
Scenario 2: Long data that needs pivot_wider()

Sometimes the data is too long and you need separate columns.

Example:

country	year	metric	value
USA	2020	population	331
USA	2020	gdp	21000
Canada	2020	population	38
Canada	2020	gdp	1700

Maybe you need a scatterplot:

x-axis = population
y-axis = gdp

For a scatterplot, you need population and gdp as separate columns.

So you use:

data_wide <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = metric,
    values_from = value
  )

This makes:

country	year	population	gdp
USA	2020	331	21000
Canada	2020	38	1700

Use pivot_wider() when one column contains variable names that need to become separate columns.

Pattern:

data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = column_with_future_column_names,
    values_from = column_with_values
  )

Memory trick:

pivot_longer() = more rows, fewer columns
pivot_wider() = fewer rows, more columns
Scenario 3: Bar chart of totals

Image clue:

You see bars comparing categories.

Example final chart:

Total revenue by store

You probably need:

group_by(store) %>%
summarize(total_revenue = sum(revenue))

Full pattern:

plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(store) %>%
  summarize(total_revenue = sum(revenue), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = store, y = total_revenue)) +
  geom_col()

Important difference:

Use geom_col() when your data already has the y-values.

Use geom_bar() when you want R to count rows for you.

Usually in your class, you will probably use:

geom_col()

because you are summarizing first.

Scenario 4: Bar chart of counts

Image clue:

The chart shows number of rows/items in each category.

Example:

Count the number of flights by airline.

You can do:

plot_data <- data %>%
  count(airline)

That gives:

airline	n
Delta	300
United	280

Then:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = airline, y = n)) +
  geom_col()

count(airline) is basically a shortcut for:

data %>%
  group_by(airline) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop")

Use this when the graph is counting how many observations are in each category.

Scenario 5: Grouped bar chart

Image clue:

Bars are side-by-side, usually with colors.

Example:

Revenue by class type, colored by location

Your final data probably needs one row per:

class_type + location

Code pattern:

plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(class_type, location) %>%
  summarize(total_revenue = sum(revenue), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = class_type, y = total_revenue, fill = location)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")

The key argument is:

position = "dodge"

That means:

Put the bars next to each other instead of stacking them.

Without it, the bars may stack on top of each other.

Scenario 6: Stacked bar chart

Image clue:

Bars are stacked, and colors show parts of a total.

Example:

Total sales by year, split by dealership type

Pattern:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = total_sales, fill = dealership_type)) +
  geom_col()

Notice there is no:

position = "dodge"

Because stacked bars are the default when you use fill.

If you want percentages:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = total_sales, fill = dealership_type)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill")

position = "fill" means:

Make each bar equal 100%.

Scenario 7: Line chart over time

Image clue:

You see a trend over days, months, quarters, or years.

Example:

Monthly revenue over time

Final data needs one row per time period:

month	total_revenue
Jan	1200
Feb	1500
Mar	1800

Pattern:

plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarize(total_revenue = sum(revenue), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = month, y = total_revenue, group = 1)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()

If there are multiple lines:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = month, y = total_revenue, color = location, group = location)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()

Important:

For line charts, you often need group.

If there is one line:

group = 1

If there are multiple lines:

group = location
Scenario 8: Scatterplot

Image clue:

You see dots, not bars, comparing two numeric variables.

Example:

Relationship between ad spending and revenue

Pattern:

ggplot(data, aes(x = ad_spend, y = revenue)) +
  geom_point()

Add color if the dots are grouped:

ggplot(data, aes(x = ad_spend, y = revenue, color = region)) +
  geom_point()

Add a trend line:

ggplot(data, aes(x = ad_spend, y = revenue)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

Scatterplot usually does not need group_by() first unless the image is using averages or summaries.

Scenario 9: Faceted chart

Image clue:

The chart is split into multiple mini charts.

Your dealership chart had one panel for each year.

Pattern:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = total_sold, y = dealership)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ year)

or:

facet_grid(. ~ year)

Use facet_wrap() for a flexible layout.

Use facet_grid() when you want strict rows/columns.

Common patterns:

facet_wrap(~ year)

means:

Make one chart per year.

facet_grid(region ~ year)

means:

Rows are region, columns are year.

Scenario 10: Need to extract year/month from a date

You might see a date column like:

date
2026-01-15
2026-02-20

First make sure it is a date:

data <- data %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

Then use lubridate.

library(lubridate)

data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date, label = TRUE),
    quarter = quarter(date)
  )

If the date is text like "2017 Q1" like your dealers data, you may use string tools instead:

data <- data %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(str_sub(quarter, 1, 4)))

For "2017 Q1":

str_sub(quarter, 1, 4)

gets:

"2017"
Scenario 11: Need to filter to certain rows

Image clue:

The title says something like:

Top 10 countries in 2020
California counties only
Sales after 2018
Only single-family permits

Pattern:

data %>%
  filter(year == 2020)

Multiple conditions:

data %>%
  filter(year == 2020, state == "California")

That means both must be true.

Another way:

data %>%
  filter(year == 2020 & state == "California")

For “or”:

data %>%
  filter(state == "California" | state == "Idaho")

Better version:

data %>%
  filter(state %in% c("California", "Idaho"))

Use %in% when you want several possible values.

Scenario 12: Need top 10

Image clue:

The graph only shows the largest 10 categories.

Pattern:

plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarize(total = sum(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  slice_max(total, n = 10)

Then for a horizontal bar chart:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = total, y = reorder(category, total))) +
  geom_col()

This part:

reorder(category, total)

means:

Sort the categories by the total.

For horizontal bar charts, this is super useful.

Scenario 13: Need percentages

Image clue:

The y-axis says percent, share, proportion, or rate.

Example:

What percent of sales came from each region?

Pattern:

plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(region) %>%
  summarize(total_sales = sum(sales), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(percent = total_sales / sum(total_sales))

Then:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = region, y = percent)) +
  geom_col()

Format y-axis as percent:

library(scales)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = region, y = percent)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent)

Important idea:

sum(total_sales)

inside mutate() after summarizing means:

Add all the summarized totals together.

Then each category gets its share.

Scenario 14: Need to clean column names

Raw data may have awful names like:

"Drug Category"
"Labeler Name"
"Number of Cars Sold"
"...1"

Option 1: Rename manually:

data <- data %>%
  rename(
    drug_category = `Drug Category`,
    labeler_name = `Labeler Name`,
    cars_sold = `Number of Cars Sold`
  )

Use backticks when column names have spaces:

`Drug Category`

Option 2: Use janitor:

library(janitor)

data <- data %>%
  clean_names()

That changes:

Drug Category

into:

drug_category

This is often worth doing at the start.

Scenario 15: Need to recode confusing values

Raw data may have codes:

drug_type
1
2

But the chart wants:

drug_type
Prescription
Over the counter

Use case_when():

data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    drug_type = case_when(
      drug_type == 1 ~ "Prescription",
      drug_type == 2 ~ "Over the counter",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

Pattern:

mutate(
  new_column = case_when(
    condition1 ~ "Label 1",
    condition2 ~ "Label 2",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )
)

TRUE ~ "Other" is the fallback.

Scenario 16: Need to reorder bars

Image clue:

Bars go from biggest to smallest.

Use:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = total, y = reorder(category, total))) +
  geom_col()

If vertical bars:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = reorder(category, total), y = total)) +
  geom_col()

If you want biggest at top in a horizontal bar chart:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = total, y = reorder(category, total))) +
  geom_col()

Usually this works well.

If it is backwards, use:

reorder(category, -total)

or:

forcats::fct_reorder(category, total)

But simple reorder() is enough for most class challenges.

How to recognize what code you need from the picture
If the picture has bars

Ask:

Are bars showing totals, counts, or averages?

Totals:

summarize(total = sum(value))

Counts:

count(category)

Averages:

summarize(avg = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))

Then:

geom_col()
If the picture has lines

Ask:

What is the time variable?

Usually:

year
month
date
quarter

Then:

group_by(time)
summarize(...)
geom_line()
If the picture has dots

Ask:

What two numeric columns are being compared?

Then:

ggplot(data, aes(x = numeric1, y = numeric2)) +
  geom_point()
If the picture has multiple panels

Look for:

facet_wrap()
facet_grid()
If the picture has colors

Look for:

fill =

for bars.

color =

for points and lines.

Bars:

aes(fill = category)

Points/lines:

aes(color = category)
The most common argument mistakes
filter()

Correct:

filter(year == 2020)

Wrong:

filter(year = 2020)

Why?

One equals sign assigns. Two equals signs tests equality.

Use:

==

inside filter().

select()

Correct:

select(year, dealership, sales)

This keeps columns.

You do not use quotes usually.

mutate()

Correct:

mutate(total = price * quantity)

This creates or changes columns.

Pattern:

mutate(new_column = formula)
group_by() plus summarize()

Correct:

group_by(region) %>%
summarize(total_sales = sum(sales), .groups = "drop")

The column you group by stays as categories.

The column you summarize becomes a new number.

ggplot(aes())

This is a big one.

Correct:

ggplot(data, aes(x = region, y = total_sales)) +
  geom_col()

Inside aes(), put column names.

Outside aes(), put fixed choices.

Correct:

geom_col(fill = "blue")

because every bar is blue.

Correct:

ggplot(data, aes(x = region, y = total_sales, fill = region))

because the fill color changes based on the region column.

Wrong-ish:

ggplot(data, aes(x = region, y = total_sales, fill = "blue"))

That makes "blue" act like a category, not a color setting.

Your test cheat sheet

Here are the code chunks you should have ready in your brain.

Read and inspect
library(tidyverse)

data <- read_csv("LINK_OR_FILE")

glimpse(data)
names(data)
View(data)
Clean names
library(janitor)

data <- data %>%
  clean_names()
Rename one weird column
data <- data %>%
  rename(new_name = old_name)

For weird names:

data <- data %>%
  rename(new_name = `Old Name With Spaces`)
Pivot longer
data_long <- data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = columns_to_stack,
    names_to = "category_name",
    values_to = "value_name"
  )

Example:

data_long <- data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -quarter,
    names_to = "dealership",
    values_to = "cars_sold"
  )
Pivot wider
data_wide <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = category_column,
    values_from = value_column
  )
Summarize totals
plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarize(total = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
Summarize averages
plot_data <- data %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarize(avg = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
Count rows
plot_data <- data %>%
  count(category)
Basic bar chart
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = category, y = total)) +
  geom_col()
Horizontal bar chart
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = total, y = reorder(category, total))) +
  geom_col()
Line chart
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = total, group = 1)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
Multiple-line chart
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = total, color = category, group = category)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
Scatterplot
ggplot(data, aes(x = variable1, y = variable2)) +
  geom_point()
Facets
facet_wrap(~ category)

or:

facet_grid(. ~ category)
Let’s make this into real practice

I’ll give you a fake image description and fake raw data shape. You tell me the first 2–3 coding moves. I will correct you.

Practice Challenge 1

The final image is:

A horizontal bar chart showing the top 10 counties by total housing permits in 2010. The bars are ordered from smallest at the bottom to largest at the top. The x-axis is total permits. The y-axis is county name.

The raw data has columns:

state
county
year
permit_type
value

Example rows:

state	county	year	permit_type	value
CA	Los Angeles	2010	Single Family	1200
CA	Orange	2010	Single Family	900
CA	Los Angeles	2010	Multi Family	400
ID	Madison	2010	Single Family	80

Your goal is California only, year 2010, total permits by county, top 10.

Start with this:

permits %>%

Your job: write the next few lines to filter to California and 2010, then group by county.

Do not write the plot yet.

Use this shape:

permits %>%
  filter(_____, _____) %>%
  group_by(_____)

Send your code, and I’ll correct it like a teacher.
